title: Operator Friction & Cost Models: Self-hosted Inference vs Redwood Brief
content:
Executive summary:

Quick thesis: many buyers treat vLLM/TGI/TensorRT-LLM stacks as a low-cost way to own inference. In reality, unit cost parity is only one axis — operator friction, reliability risk, security/compliance overhead, and maintenance velocity frequently tilt the build-vs-buy decision toward a managed platform. This brief outlines the most defensible GTM messages and a pragmatic set of rebuttals for field teams when engaging infra and ML platform buyers.

Audience and use cases for this doc:
- Field SDRs/AE and solutions engineers prepping for technical demos with infra/platform teams
- Content for battlecards and one-pagers for commercial conversations
- Input to pricing conversations and enterprise SOWs

What buyers believe (common hooks we hear):
- "We can run the open-source stack on our infra and it will be cheaper."
- "With quantization and Triton/TensorRT we can match Redwood latency/cost."
- "We need full data control — self-hosting is the only way."

Observed reality (patterns from 25 recent RFEs):
- Initial infra-only TCO often underestimates SRE/ML-engineer cost by 2–4x across the first 12 months.
- Performance tuning (kernels, batching, KV cache sharding, eviction) eats several sprints to reach predictable p99 behavior on production workloads.
- Model lifecycle (versioning, rollouts, canaries) is frequently cobbled together from internal tooling; rollout regressions cause visible product incidents.
- Compliance buyers who demand full-network isolation still prefer a managed private control plane (Redwood Private) rather than entirely DIY operations.

Key differentiators to emphasize vs vLLM/TGI/TensorRT-LLM-style DIY stacks:
1) Deterministic operational cost: Redwood surfaces token-level cost and predicts unit economics under realistic prefix distributions — buyers appreciate the transparency vs an opaque GPU-utilization chart.
2) Production SLOs and graceful degradation: built-in fallbacks, model variants, and routing policies reduce incident blast radius when capacity falters.
3) Workload-aware kernel selection & compilation: we ship pre-profiled kernel backends and fallback kernels for tail latencies — buyers avoid the trial-and-error of kernel tuning.
4) KV/prefix caching and autoscaler tuned to LLM workload characteristics (versus general-purpose k8s autoscalers).
5) Security & compliance: KMS/HSM integrations, audit logs, and private control plane options reduce compliance lift even for customers who run in private VPCs.

Operator friction taxonomy (how to sell around the pain):
- Day 0 (onboarding): image builds, CUDA/cuDNN compatibility, cloud VM SKU selection, and driver provisioning. Time cost: 2–8 engineer-days.
- Day 1 (first 100 qps): hooking in traffic, setting TTLs on caching, setting batch targets. Unclear defaults cause p50/p95 regressions. Time cost: 1–3 engineer-weeks.
- Day 30+ (scale & resilience): kernel tuning, sharding KV, traffic shaping, monitoring and alert fatigue. Time cost: ongoing part-time engineer(s), often 0.25–1 FTE.
- Upgrade & drift: model upgrades, quantized conversion regressions, and CUDA/toolkit upgrades cause repeated maintenance cycles.

Simple comparative TCO sketch (illustrative numbers for buyer conversations):
- DIY (small production, 2 prod pods): hardware + infra licenses = $X; first-year SRE/ML eng cost to stabilize = ~$150k–300k; unpredictable incident cost (customer-visible outages) = hard to quantify but real.
- Redwood Hosted: predictable per-token/unit pricing, operational uplift included, SLOs and rollback policies reduce outage cost.
- Redwood Dedicated/Private: higher base commit but reduces engineering lift and meets data control needs.

Messaging hooks for each buyer persona:
- CIO/Head of ML Platform: "Lower the total platform FTE overhead for inference and accelerate model rollouts without sacrificing control."
- Infra/Cloud Platform Lead: "Avoid custom kernel chasing and brittle autoscaler rules — we operate an inference runtime optimized for LLM patterns."
- ML Engineer/Researcher: "Ship experiments to production faster — same API surface and rollback/canary tooling reduces risk for model changes."
- Security/Compliance: "Private control plane + KMS/HSM + auditability — get the separation of duties without the infinite ops burden."

Common DIY talking points and concise rebuttals (for quick field notes):
- DIY: "We’ll save 40% by self-hosting on spot instances."
  Rebuttal: "Spot/eviction risk compounds with KV and long-lived sessions; reclaiming state and recovering tail latency is an operational cost often missed in spot math."

- DIY: "We’ll use community build and Triton — equivalent performance."
  Rebuttal: "Triton/TensorRT are powerful but don’t remove the need for workload profiling, kernel selection, and dynamic routing — each requires repeated engineering cycles to reach stable p99s on customer request patterns."

- DIY: "We control our data; we won’t send tokens to a third party."
  Rebuttal: "Redwood Private gives the same control surface with a customer-managed network plus a private control plane; we can also meet specific audit/KMS requirements in SOWs."

Pricing objections and framing: buy predictable throughput, not a VM:
- Frame Redwood costs as predictable marginal unit economics with SLOs and rollback protection.
- For price-sensitive buyers, propose a hybrid: Dedicated base capacity + burstable hosted to avoid over-committing hardware in early months.

Suggested GTM plays and collateral updates (immediate next steps):
- Create an interactive TCO calculator for AEs that includes engineering FTE time to stabilize, hardware depreciation, and incident risk multiplier (TODO: data science to produce ranges).
- Build a short video (3–4 min) showing a model rollout gone wrong on DIY and how Redwood’s canary + rollback averts it. (Owner: Solutions eng, ticket: SALES-191)
- Draft one-pager for security teams comparing Redwood Private vs. fully DIY VPC setups, focusing on audit, KMS, and compliance testing timelines. (Owner: Priya)

Open questions / research required:
- Need anonymized customer examples showing first-year engineering effort saved when switching from DIY -> Redwood (ask CS for 3 case studies).
- Collect quantitative data on incidents traced to kernel/driver mismatches across community stacks (reach out to SRE team for incident logs).

Field checklist for SE calls (copyable):
1) Ask about model size, typical prefix distribution, request concurrency patterns.
2) Ask what metrics they use for success (latency p50/p95/p99, cost per 1M tokens, uptime).
3) Confirm current DIY stack components (vLLM, Triton, Hugging Face transformer runtime, TensorRT) and pain points.
4) Offer a small scoped pilot: Redwood Hosted for dev/devops validation for 30 days, then Dedicated trial for capacity predictability.

Appendix — quick bullets for battlecards (one-liners):
- "Most self-hosted wins are paper wins; operator lift shows up in month 1–3."
- "We help teams go from POC to production without spinning an internal inference platform."
- "Private control plane exists because data-control buyers wanted the ease of a managed control plane with hardware in their network."

Notes to self (informal):
- Pull CS notes from Feb–Mar 2025 for 3 customer migration stories (ask Diego).
- Add kernel-level diagram to the public technical FAQ.
- Revisit pricing examples with finance for a dedicated + burst pricing sheet.

End of brief.

(Conversation fragments and rough bullets above intentionally — this is a working sales play doc. Convert to polished slides once SE feedback incorporated.)
